context_sources.name: Fleming, domestic financial policies under fixed and floating rates
Klein and Shambaugh, exchange rate regimes

limitations: Equation systems are printed as flattened braces, so term order is reconstructed from the prose.
Table 1 rows are misaligned: descriptions sit several rows away from their symbols.
Several pages are figure-only and contribute no text.
The ANOVA output is described but no statistic, p-value or coefficient is printed.
Pages 22, 25 and 27 carry almost no extractable text.

tasks: Build a model of the financial system that includes digital currency
Judge a global decentralized market and design a general currency
Name what limits or helps growth, access, security and stability
Say how countries change their banking models and what follows
Add oversight, study long-run effects, and consider dropping national currency

section_map.summary: Three views, a virtual country, two regimes, a world bank.
Seven tasks from viability to abandoning national currency.
Cobb-Douglas split, then the LM curve.
Fixed and floating, Sweden and Israel.

contributions.summary: A closed-form split of money between the two currencies.
Capital-flow parameters added to the external balance.
The same diagnosis mapped to opposite policies under two regimes.

dependency_graph.handoff: The two individual holdings sum to national money demand
The LM rate must agree with the IS rate at the internal balance
Goods-market output enters net exports on the external balance
The money-market rate is what capital flows compare with the foreign rate

assumptions.summary: Depreciation and retained profits are zero, so five income measures coincide.
The digital currency supply is fixed and infinitely divisible.
No exchange control, and the buy price equals the sell price.

data_and_preprocessing.summary: Sweden under a fixed rate, Israel under a floating rate.
Thailand and Mexico used as robustness cases.
An appendix of real data results, with no readable figures in the text.

models.summary: Cobb-Douglas choice between the two currencies.
LM curve with digital and traditional supply added.

verification.summary: ANOVA on the linear regressions, coefficients called small.
The same policy logic applied to Thailand and Mexico.

results_trace.summary: Sweden should tighten both policies; both curves shift left.
Israel should tighten money only; the rate does part of the work.
Thailand tightens spending and loosens money; Mexico tightens money.

writing_logic.summary: One of the two paths is dropped in a sentence, so the rest of the paper has a single case.
Three shocks are ranked by how hard they hit, not merely listed.
A war example carries the capital-flow argument.

language_observations.summary: A country that does not exist is defined by three identifications.
An intervention is said to move the money supply by several times itself.
A floating rate is credited with reaching balance on its own.
Small coefficients are read as insensitivity to outliers.

visualization_observations.summary: Figure 1: the individual trade-off and the points off the curve.
Figure 2: what makes the LM curve flat.
Figure 3: why the LM curve shifts right.
Figures 6 to 8: policy mechanisms under a fixed rate.
Figure 9: the three curves together for Sweden and Israel.
Figure 10: ANOVA on the linear regressions.
Figure 11: the model on Thailand and Mexico.

judge_relevance_hypotheses.summary: The ANOVA is called decisive, but no statistic or p-value is printed.
A virtual country stands in for the issuer, so every result depends on a fiction.
The paper admits it only models two countries.

weaknesses.summary: Every equation is linear, which the paper says cannot describe some economies.
The sensitivity claim rests on coefficients that are never shown.

independent_extensions.summary: Estimate the preference exponents from survey or transaction data.
Fit gamma and sigma and report them.
Extend the external balance from two countries to many.

candidate_rule_impacts.summary: Give each policy tool the target it moves most.
Let capital flows set the slope of the external balance.

unresolved_questions.question: What values do the preference exponents take?
What ANOVA statistics support the insensitivity claim?
What regulations would the proposed world bank actually enforce?
